data.title: Fed likely to need to raise rates amid worsening inflation: Daly
data.description:
Key points:
  • Services inflation moving in the wrong direction, Daly says
  • Daly says producers increasingly want to pass higher costs to consumers
  • Consumer may be starting to run out of gas, Daly says

By Ann Saphir

San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Friday that her "bias" is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, particularly with services inflation moving in the wrong direction and some signs of inflation persistence.

"We're going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving," Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event. "Producers are telling us more and more that they're running out of room to take it out of margins, and they really want to consider passing along this to consumers. So that's the inflationary impulse we want to avoid."

The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3% month over month in each of the last three months. That's far higher than the 0.2% or less that would be consistent with year-over-year inflation at 2%, the Fed's target.

Daly, like several other policymakers, said she's particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing is "not moving in the correct direction," which is particularly troubling because that slice of inflation tends to be sticky.

"That's a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, maybe they're going to pass that along to customers," she said.

The Fed raised its policy rate in September but held it steady in October, and financial markets are betting heavily on quarter-point interest-rate hikes at each of the Fed's December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings. Daly said she feels markets understand how the Fed sets rates in response to economic conditions, without remarking specifically on the timing of coming rate hikes.

Daly said she is also paying close attention to consumer spending, which accounts for most of the US economy, as the December meeting approaches.

"Consumer spending remains just surprisingly resilient; you just haven't seen a pullback, so I think that's the piece of information that I'm really looking for in the next one to two to three months: what happens in that, especially around the holiday season, do we see consumers giving up or do we see them keeping going even if prices rise?" Daly said.

"Sitting here in Las Vegas...we're just starting to hear that the consumer may be running out of gas. And we're hearing that now in other states, not just Nevada."

data.title: Will Nvidia Affirm Huang-Era Financial Forecasts? (and Other Earnings Questions) — WSJ
data.description:
By Ed Ballard

Is it too early to be thinking about Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday? No! It's never too early to be thinking about Nvidia's next earnings report, and this one is important.

Here is what Morningstar analyst Brian Colello is on the lookout for, besides any commentary on the current turmoil over Jensen Huang's love life and the surrounding foreign-intelligence probe.

Guidance. Will the company stand by forecasts it issued under Jensen Huang's leadership? They include company-specific targets, such as 70% revenue growth for its 2028 financial year, and industry projections such as $3 to $4 trillion in global AI spending by 2030.

Politics. Did the U.S. midterm elections, in which many Democrats won on anti-data-center platforms, lead to any pause in orders or concern about a slowdown in demand?

Financing. Will there be more commentary on Nvidia's financial support for some of its partners? Colello thinks the company has "explained its exposure well to date," but rising interest rates complicate the picture.

As for the results themselves, "we'd be stunned if Nvidia provided an earnings miss or weak forecast," Colello said, pointing to strong capital spending by big tech companies. But the underlying business is "a bit secondary for this quarter."

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Widow of Late Campbell's Chairman Asks $170 Million for Miami Beach Mansion — WSJ
data.description:
By Katherine Clarke

A waterfront Miami Beach, Fla., mansion built by George Sherman, the late former chairman of soup maker Campbell's, is coming on the market for $170 million. If it fetches that price, it would be one of the Miami area's priciest-ever home sales.

The property is located at the tip of La Gorce Island, a guard-gated community on Biscayne Bay that has drawn some of Miami's wealthiest residents.

George and his wife, Betsy Sherman, bought the 1.2-acre lot for $17 million in 2006 and finished the house around 2015, property records show. The mansion spans more than 18,000 square feet with eight bedrooms.

Betsy, who also owns significant estates in Baltimore, and in Camden, Maine, said she is moving into an apartment following her husband's death in 2021. "I feel as if it's time for a family to be enjoying it, so I'm reluctantly parting ways," she said.

The Miami-Dade County record was set earlier this year when Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, paid $170 million for an under-construction mansion on Indian Creek island.

George was named Campbell's chairman in 2001 and retired from the role in 2004. He was also previously president of Black & Decker's power-tools and home-improvement group.

The Shermans had a long history in Miami Beach and made it their primary home in later years. Before buying on La Gorce, they owned a condo on Fisher Island, which they purchased from Oprah Winfrey, Betsy said. They eventually sold that apartment because she found herself yearning for a property with a yard, she said.

"We were up so high you could never hear the swishing of the wind through the trees, and I missed that," she said.

For the La Gorce house, she envisioned something more contemporary than the "Mediterranean dream" of Fisher Island.

"I wanted the house to be the quiet part and the view to be the spectacular part," she said. "So that sort of lends itself to a more contemporary, clean look."

She said the home was designed to fit her family's needs at the time. A children's bunk room was directly across the hall from the primary bedroom, so the grandchildren could run across the hall if they had a bad dream.

Now, Betsy said, she is now moving back to Fisher Island.

Listing agent Jill Hertzberg of Coldwell Banker Realty, who is listing the property with her children Danny and Hillary Hertzberg, said the value of the property stems in large part from its location on a "primo lot" on the island.

La Gorce Island has commanded some of the highest prices in the Miami area. In 2024, entrepreneur Anand Khubani paid $100 million for three contiguous properties there.

data.title: Anthropic Chief Tells Jamie Dimon He Hopes IPO Will 'Underpromise and Overdeliver' — WSJ
data.description:
By Kate Clark

Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei said that when it comes to the artificial-intelligence giant's planned initial public offering, he hopes the company will "underpromise and overdeliver."

Amodei made the comments while speaking Friday in a livestreamed fireside chat with JPMorgan Chase Chief Executive Jamie Dimon at the bank's Manhattan headquarters. The audience included existing and prospective Anthropic investors as well as Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and Amodei's wife, Cami Clark.

The maker of the popular Claude chatbot is targeting a valuation of roughly $1.33 trillion or more, and its shares are expected to begin trading Thursday. JPMorgan is one of the more than 20 underwriters on the deal. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering.

It has been a wild ride for Anthropic, which launched its IPO into a volatile market. AI-related stocks collapsed earlier this month, prompting the Nasdaq composite to lose $2.5 trillion in a single day, as investors questioned whether lofty return expectations will come to fruition. Stocks recovered some since, but the shocking exit of former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang this week following his affair with a suspected Chinese spy hit shares in Nvidia and caused more investor angst.

Nvidia is both a supplier of chips to Anthropic and is set, along with other tech giants, to take a large stake in the company alongside the IPO.

"We're not super fussed on when exactly, what month, what market conditions we go public into," Amodei told Dimon.

As recently as a few months ago, Wall Street expected the offering to value Anthropic at as high as $2 trillion. Those expectations dropped to around $1.5 trillion more recently and then below that following the market selloff earlier this month, which prompted some large investors to push Anthropic to lower the targeted valuation.

Amodei suggested that the company is conservatively pricing its offering, telling Dimon that throughout the process, he has gotten varying versions of advice to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's really worth."

Anthropic said earlier this week that it plans to sell 825 million shares at a price range of $70 to $78 a share. The price range or offering size is likely to be increased after strong investor demand so far for its shares, according to people familiar with the matter.

That puts the company on track to raise over $61 billion at the midpoint of its current target range, plus a $26 billion private placement from big investors including Google.

Anthropic could top the size of SpaceX's record-breaking June offering if it raises more than $75 billion. (Dimon also hosted a fireside chat with Elon Musk ahead of SpaceX's IPO.)

Amodei also addressed Anthropic's lofty goals, including to find cures to diseases.

"It sounds starry eyed, it sounds crazy," he said. "I really do believe it can be done."

Amodei called investing in computing power the "deepest business dilemma that the company faces," given the massive investment required.

data.title: With earnings expected to slow, Goldman strategists eye value in growth
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq falls ~1.1%, S&P down ~0.6%, Dow edges red
  • Tech is weakest S&P 500 sector; consumer staples leads gainers
  • Dollar slightly green, gold edges up; US crude ~flat; bitcoin down >3%
  • US 10-year Treasury yield rises to ~5.14%

WITH EARNINGS EXPECTED TO SLOW, GOLDMAN STRATEGISTS EYE VALUE IN GROWTH

While describing 2026 as "the year of strong earnings," Goldman Sachs is preparing investors for sharply slower growth in 2027, but its strategists say in their latest research report that they're expecting equities to continue to rise, albeit with some big bumps along the way.

The report, led by Peter Oppenheimer, the firm's chief global equity strategist, pins slowing growth on issues such as a likely peak in AI capital spending and a still-elevated cost of capital.

In the US, they estimate that earnings growth will sink to 11% in 2027 from an estimated 36% in 2026 for S&P 500 CBOE:SPX companies. In Europe, they see growth dropping to 7% next year from an estimated 18% in 2026 for the STOXX 600 index . And, in emerging markets, they expect growth to tumble to 26% from a jaw-dropping 66% estimate for 2026 for the MSCI emerging markets index CBOE:EFS.

The change, as per Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research, looks even more dramatic in graphical form:

With that in mind, the strategists expect "investors to seek companies that can sustain growth as it becomes more scarce."

Since equities have de-rated sharply already and valuations are more attractive, with the prospect of slower nominal economic and earnings growth, lower bond yields, inflation and oil prices, Oppenheimer says he expects "equities to continue to rise, but with high volatility."

Looking to recent weeks, he notes that the fall in equities, due to concerns around AI, "has rapidly priced in the prospect of weaker growth rates, and the sharp sector and factor rotations within equities have pushed up the valuation of Defensive and Value parts of the market."

With that, the group says it is focused on balancing growth with selective defensives and beneficiaries of lower bond yields.

For example, they point to attractive opportunities in long-duration growth companies, "which should become more valuable as growth rates slow, particularly US Hyperscalers, which continue to enjoy strong (although slower) earnings growth and balance sheets."

"While forecast returns are highest in Asia, we focus on risk-adjusted returns and are overweight the US and Japan, neutral in Asia and EM, and underweight Europe, reflecting relative growth, profitability and valuation opportunities," the strategists said.

But they caution that risks "are becoming more two-sided" as bonds, oil prices and AI capex shifts could all increase volatility.

data.title: Paraguay adds criminal association charge against ex-president Peña
data.description:
By Daniela Desantis

The Paraguay prosecutor's office has added a criminal association charge against recently impeached President Santiago Peña and former central bank officials, deepening the fallout over the collapse of digital lender ueno.

In addition to Peña, former central bank president Carlos Carvallo was charged with the offense, along with three former central bank directors and the former head of the banking regulator.

Prosecutors allege the accused formed a structure made up of executive branch and central bank officials who sought to favor interests linked to ueno and its parent company.

"From the presidency of the Republic, Santiago Peña Palacios allegedly acted as the head of the organization," prosecutors said in a charging document.

Both Peña and Carvallo, who were previously charged over alleged breach of trust and administration for personal gain and placed in pretrial detention, have denied wrongdoing.

Prosecutors allege that Peña used his position as president to influence decisions by government agencies and state-owned entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at ueno, despite maintaining financial ties to the lender.

Prosecutors also allege that Peña issued public and institutional directives benefiting the digital lender, suppressed insolvency alerts and received illicit payments.

Peña was replaced on November 6 by his vice president, Pedro Alliana, after a swift impeachment process in wake of the ueno bank collapse.

data.title: FTC Sues to Block Proposed $3.5 Billion Covetrus-MWI Merger
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Covetrus has been sued by the Federal Trade Commission to block the company from acquiring rival MWI Veterinary Supply.

Covetrus, which provides supplies to veterinarians, agreed in February to acquire Cencora's MWI animal-health business in a deal worth $3.5 billion.

The FTC is alleging the transaction would merge two of the biggest suppliers in the vet-clinic distribution industry, potentially driving up costs and hurting competition.

Covetrus responded to the suit Friday saying the merger would improve the economics of veterinary practices. By combining, Covetrus and MWI would make it easier and more efficient for vets to access products, the company said.

In its suit, the FTC said the emergence of Vetcove, an online platform allowing vets to compare prices across distributors, has fueled more pricing competition among suppliers. The market concentration that would allegedly occur from a merger renders the deal unlawful under antitrust law, the FTC said.

The FTC vote to authorize staff to seek a permanent injunction to block the proposed deal was 2-0.

Covetrus said it was confident in the merits of the proposed deal and that it was prepared to defend them in court.

data.title: Stocks fall with tech, Nvidia concerns; US dollar climbs
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq leads Wall Street indexes lower
  • Oil prices on track for 2nd weekly fall
  • Dollar extends gains for 4th day

By Caroline Valetkevitch and Elizabeth Howcroft

Stock indexes were mostly lower on Friday as technology shares sold off amid fresh concerns about US chipmaker Nvidia , while the dollar climbed to a fresh 19-month high.

The Nasdaq fell more than 1%, leading declines on Wall Street, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index down 4% and shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom sharply lower. Nvidia shares were down 3%.

Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday as Nvidia CEO could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader AI industry and supply chain given his push to preserve access to the Chinese market and close ties with US President Donald Trump.

The US Justice Department said it does not know whether the Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal was a spy.

Inflation worries remained in focus. Investors absorbed a report showing the US October Producer Price Index for final demand was slightly softer than expected, but still shot up 6.5% year over year. It followed a hotter-than-expected US consumer prices reading earlier this week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 120.15 points, or 0.23%, to 52,176.94, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX fell 63.99 points, or 0.84%, to 7,528.41 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 356.51 points, or 1.40%, to 25,009.58.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe EURONEXT:IACWI fell 7.66 points, or 0.69%, to 1,108.61. The pan-European STOXX 600 index ended up 0.02%, registering a gain for the week.

AI-related shares in China dropped after Huang's exit, but indexes in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea gained overnight as traders played down concerns about its impact on the AI boom.

A more than 12-hour outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams was still affecting communications for businesses and governments globally on Friday, forcing some to revert to fax machines and halting at least one bond repurchase in Europe.

US 2-YEAR YIELDS HEAD FOR LARGEST WEEKLY RISE IN OVER TWO YEARS

The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro,

rose 0.13% to 103.35, and hit its highest level since April 2025. It was also on track for a fourth straight day of gains.

The euro was down 0.17% at $1.1034. Against the Japanese yen , the dollar strengthened 0.03% to 159.9.

Treasury yields briefly dipped after the PPI data, but interest-rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yields were on track for the largest weekly increase in over two years.

Traders this week have been ramping up bets on faster interest rate increases following the consumer price data and hawkish Federal Reserve official commentary.

"Inflation is stubbornly high and the Fed's going to need to act a little bit quicker and a little bit more aggressively," said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities.

Fed funds futures traders are pricing in an 11% chance of a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, which was seen as having zero probability a week ago, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool.

The 2-year note (US2YT=RR) yield was last down 0.94 basis point at 4.855%. It earlier reached 4.892%, the highest since October 14, and is headed for the biggest weekly increase since the first week of October 2024.

Oil prices edged lower and were set for a second straight weekly decline as Washington's focus on blockading Iran and ramping up other economic pressures allayed fears of renewed direct conflict. US crude fell 0.34% to $88.44 a barrel and Brent fell to $95.70 per barrel, down 0.14% on the day.
